pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 2-digit using formal SHORT division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context; and CHOOSE short vs long division.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using … short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.2 fluent multi-digit division; 5.NBT.6 division by 2-digit divisors — method choice is a UK curriculum emphasis.
• Operational details — the distinctive skill is METHOD SELECTION: short division by a 2-digit divisor is efficient when the divisor is 'friendly' (e.g. 16, or a divisor whose multiples the child knows/can derive quickly, 3648÷16), doing the multiply-subtract mentally at each place; long division is safer when the divisor is awkward and mental multiples are hard. This is exemplary of strategic tool choice. Children need both methods secure, then judgement about which fits. Remainder interpretation (as decimal/fraction in measurement contexts) carries over. Estimate first and check by multiplying back.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): short division by a friendly 2-digit divisor (e.g. ÷12, ÷15). Tier B (age 10–11): 3648÷16 by short division and interpret the remainder in context. Tier C (age 11): justify choosing short vs long division for given calculations and explain the trade-off.
bestPractices: Teach method CHOICE explicitly — short division when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold mentally; long division when they aren't — as a case of strategic tool selection.
Secure both methods first, then give mixed sets where the child must decide and justify the method.
Support mental multiples of the divisor (derive 16×3 etc.) so the compressed short-division steps are reliable.
Carry over flexible remainder interpretation (decimal/fraction in measurement, round by context).
Estimate first and check by multiplying the quotient back; compare efficiency of the two methods on the same calculation.
keyRepresentations: Short-division ('bus stop') layout with a 2-digit divisor
Side-by-side short vs long division of the same calculation (efficiency comparison)
Divisor multiples list to support the mental steps
Bar model / number line for remainder interpretation
commonMisconceptions: Forcing short division with an awkward divisor and making mental-multiple errors (should choose long division).
Carry/remainder errors in the compressed steps because the mental multiplication is insecure.
Not interpreting the remainder appropriately for the context.
Believing one method is always 'better' rather than choosing by the numbers.
Place-value slips when the divisor doesn't fit into a leading digit.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal short division where appropriate, choose between short and long division based on how 'friendly' the divisor is, and interpret remainders according to context (as a whole number, fraction, or decimal). The core new skill is strategic METHOD SELECTION once both methods are secure, supported by mental multiples of the divisor and by estimating and checking with multiplication.

activities.title: Method-chooser: the same division, two ways
feedback: 3648÷16 = 228 exactly; if your answer isn't near your estimate of ~225, recheck a step.
If a short-division step went wrong, check whether your mental multiple of the divisor was correct (e.g. 16×3=48) — insecure multiples are a common cause of carry errors.

Once the quotient has started, if the divisor doesn't fit into the current part, write a zero in that place of the quotient and carry any amount on; otherwise the quotient will have the wrong number of digits (4080÷17 = 240 is a good example — the zero in the ones place matters because 17 does not go into the final 0).
If you found short division error-prone with ÷17, that friction is the point: it shows why an awkward divisor often calls for long division.
activities.rationale: Method choice may be learned effectively by doing the same division both ways and experiencing the efficiency/reliability trade-off, with support for the mental multiples that short division compresses. Securing both methods first, then giving mixed problems where the learner decides and justifies, is proposed to build the judgement the Year 6 standard targets.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context.
Choosing short vs long division by the divisor's friendliness is a case of strategic tool selection; both methods should be secure first.
learnerActions: Solve 3648÷16 using short division ('bus stop' layout), using a list of multiples of 16 (16, 32, 48, 160, 1600, …) to support the multiply-subtract step at each place.
Solve the SAME calculation 3648÷16 using long division, writing out each multiply-subtract step.
Compare the two side by side and state which was quicker for THIS divisor and why.
Now try a divisor many learners find awkward, e.g. 4080÷17, by short division; notice whether and where holding multiples of 17 mentally becomes error-prone.
Solve 4080÷17 again by long division and compare how reliable each felt.
State a rule of thumb in your own words: when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold, short division is efficient; when they are hard, long division is safer.
Estimate first (e.g. 3600÷16 ≈ 225) and check the final answer by multiplying the quotient back (228×16 = 3648?).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether short or long division is the better tool depends on how friendly the divisor is, not on habit — and you can experience this trade-off by doing the same calculation both ways. Both methods are legitimate; the skill is choosing and justifying.

activities.title: Justify the method for a mixed set
feedback: A good justification names the divisor's friendliness, e.g. 'multiples of 15 are easy (15, 30, 45…), so short division is efficient.'
If you claimed one method is always best, revisit the awkward divisor (e.g. ÷17 or ÷29) — that case shows why judgement beats a fixed rule.
Always estimate first so a slipped step is caught (e.g. 2925÷15 ≈ 3000÷15 = 200, 5887÷29 ≈ 6000÷30 = 200; the exact answers are 195 and 203).
activities.rationale: Mixed sets requiring a decision plus justification target the distinctive UK curriculum emphasis on method selection, rather than execution alone. A Socratic 'which method suits these numbers, and why?' framing is proposed to build selection judgement.
sourceClaims: Choosing short vs long division by the divisor's friendliness is a case of strategic tool selection; both methods should be secure first.
6.NS.2 requires fluent multi-digit division; 5.NBT.6 develops 2-digit-divisor division — UK adds explicit short/long method choice.
learnerActions: For each calculation in a mixed set (e.g. 3648÷16, 4080÷17, 2925÷15, 5887÷29), decide whether short or long division suits it before computing.
Write one sentence explaining your choice, referring to whether the divisor's multiples are easy to derive.
Carry out the division with your chosen method, then estimate and check by multiplying back.
Answer: is any ONE method always 'better'? Explain why not, using an example from your set.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategic tool choice means matching the method to the numbers; no single method is universally superior, and whether a divisor is 'friendly' depends on which multiples you can derive quickly.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder in context
feedback: 5 m ÷ 16 gives each piece = 5/16 m = 0.3125 m; writing '0 m r5' misses what the leftover means when sharing a length.
Ask 'what does the leftover stand for here?' — sharing the remainder equally means each share gets remainder ÷ divisor more units (e.g. 5/16 m each); convert to a decimal for a length.
In a 'how many buses?' context the remainder usually forces rounding UP; in a 'how many full boxes?' context it forces rounding DOWN.
activities.rationale: Flexible remainder interpretation (decimal/fraction in measurement, rounding by context) is an explicit standard requirement and a common failure point; a bar model or number line makes the meaning of the leftover concrete.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context.
learnerActions: Solve a measurement problem where the remainder must be expressed appropriately, e.g. '5 m of ribbon is shared into 16 equal pieces — how long is each piece?'
Share the leftover too: remainder over divisor gives the fraction of a metre added to each piece (here 5/16 m), then convert it to a decimal length.
For a different context (e.g. buses needed to carry people, or full boxes that can be filled), decide whether to round up, round down, or keep a remainder, and explain why.
Use a bar model or number line to show what the leftover represents before writing it as a fraction/decimal.
activities.intendedInsight: A remainder is not always written as 'r n' — the context dictates whether it becomes a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding, so you must interpret what the leftover means.

activities.title: Check your understanding
feedback: For method choice, the reason matters as much as the answer: short division often fits ÷16 because its multiples are easy for many learners to hold; ÷17 is often awkward because many learners find its multiples harder to derive mentally.
For the fill-in step, verify your mental multiple of the divisor and that the quotient has the right number of digits.
For the remainder item, pick the fraction/decimal form when a measurement context demands it, not 'r n'.
activities.rationale: Selected-response and fill-in items efficiently check method appropriateness, procedural execution, and remainder interpretation. These verify recognition and single-step execution; they do not by themselves show the learner can independently choose and carry out a method on a fresh problem, so pair them with an unaided performance task.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context.
learnerActions: Choose: for 3648÷16 versus 4080÷17, which calculation better suits short division, and give the reason.
Fill in the missing step of a partially worked short-division ('bus stop') layout, including writing a zero in the quotient where the divisor doesn't fit a place.
Select the correctly interpreted remainder for a measurement context (e.g. the length of each piece as a fraction or decimal) rather than a whole-number 'r' form.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise the appropriate method, execute a short-division step correctly, and interpret a remainder for its context.

constraints: Secure BOTH short and long division before asking learners to choose between them; method selection presupposes fluent execution of each.
Support mental multiples of the divisor (e.g. deriving 16×3) so the compressed short-division steps are reliable; carry/remainder errors often trace back to insecure multiplication.

Do not teach that one method is universally 'better'; the objective is choosing by the numbers. Equally, do not frame a divisor's 'friendliness' as a fixed property — it depends on which multiples the individual learner can derive quickly.

Recognition-only and fill-in items assess method appropriateness and single steps but do not elicit independent choice-and-execution on new problems; pair them with a performance task where the learner chooses and carries out a method unaided.
A static side-by-side worked comparison is a useful reference for the trade-off but cannot let the learner choose and execute on new numbers; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective.

When interpreting remainders, the correct written form depends on the context (fraction/decimal for measurement; round up or down for discrete grouping); do not apply one remainder convention universally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources carry verified:false in the source row (the CCSS-M comparison claim and the NCETM strategic-tool-selection claim); treat the 'UK adds explicit short/long method choice' and 'friendliness dictates method' framings as informed curriculum interpretation, not independently verified fact.

Arithmetic self-check: 3648÷16 = 228 exactly (228×16 = 3648); estimate 3600÷16 = 225. 5÷16 = 0.3125 = 5/16 m. Added comparison/mixed-set divisors: 4080÷17 = 240, 2925÷15 = 195, 5887÷29 = 203 — all checked here but introduced by this rewrite and not part of the verified source; re-confirm before classroom use.

The source's claim that short division 'wins here' for ÷16 is efficiency-relative and depends on the learner's fluency with multiples of 16; retained as a learner-observed comparison, not an established comparative-efficacy result.
The original 'is best learned by doing' efficacy framing was softened to proposed/qualified wording, as no source establishes the comparative effectiveness of any medium or activity format.
The original 'possible'/static worked-comparison and Socratic conversation alternatives were preserved as scaffolds and as a justification activity respectively, each with its stated limit.

probeDeeper: How did you decide how many 16s go into the first part of 3,648?
In the ribbon problem, what does the leftover mean — and how do you write it as a length?
Estimate 3,648 ÷ 16 roughly — is your answer close?
How could you check your division answer using multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,648 ÷ 16 = 228 (exact). For 5 m ÷ 16, each piece is 0.3125 m (or 5/16 m). The teacher watches for a workable division method (chunking known multiples of 16, or short/long division) and correct interpretation of the remainder as a fraction/decimal rather than 'r something' when the context demands it.

errorPatterns.pattern: has no strategy for a two-digit divisor — stalls because 16 isn't a known table, or guesses digits of the quotient
errorPatterns.nextMove: build a short menu of easy multiples first (16, 32, 160, 1600) and subtract chunks; a two-digit divisor needs known multiples, not a memorised table.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child cannot start, or writes quotient digits with no relation to multiples of 16

errorPatterns.pattern: expresses the remainder as 'r n' when the measurement context requires a fraction/decimal
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask 'what does the leftover mean when we're sharing metres?' — the remainder over the divisor is a fraction of a piece; convert to decimal for length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer given as '0 m r5' or similar rather than 5/16 m or 0.3125 m

errorPatterns.pattern: place-value slip in short division — mishandles a digit that the divisor doesn't go into (forgets the zero in the quotient)
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist on writing a zero in the quotient when the divisor doesn't fit that place, carrying the amount on; check the quotient's magnitude by estimation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient has the wrong number of digits; e.g. drops a place when 16 won't divide a leading part

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, arithmetic slip in a multiplication/subtraction step; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child check with multiplication (228×16 = 3648?) and estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one step wrong; estimate (3600÷16 ≈ 225) flags it

responseLevels.gap: has no method for a two-digit divisor, or leaves a measurement remainder as 'r n'.
responseLevels.full: divides by the two-digit number using a secure method, interprets the remainder as a whole number, fraction, or decimal according to context, and checks with multiplication/estimation.
responseLevels.partial: completes the whole-number division with support but mishandles the remainder's interpretation, or omits a quotient zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 3,648 ÷ 16 while you watch, letting them choose their method. Then give a measurement division whose remainder must be expressed as a fraction or decimal (e.g. '5 m of ribbon shared into 16 equal pieces — how long is each?') and watch how they handle the remainder. Notice whether they lean on multiples of the divisor and how they interpret what's left over.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Dividing by a two-digit number tests whether the child can build up or use multiples of an unfamiliar divisor, and the measurement item tests remainder interpretation as fraction/decimal (not whole-number rounding). Watching the method reveals whether they have a strategy for a non-table divisor or are stuck without a times-table.
